transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-09-14
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE), Nina Grover (Redwood SE), Liam Chen (Aegis Head of ML Infra), Sofia Martinez (Aegis Senior ML Eng), Amir Khan (Aegis CTO)

Auto-generated Summary (optional):
- Deep dive on GPU runtime profiling focusing on kernel selection heuristics, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM execution trade-offs, and the role of CUDA Graphs for latency stabilization.
- Customer will provide sample model and traces; Redwood to run targeted microbenchmarks and share spreadsheet and recommended config for Dedicated / Private deployment.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We know time is tight so Carlos and Nina from our runtime team will lead the deep dive. Quick intros?
[00:07] Liam: Hey, Liam Chen, I run ML infra at Aegis. Sofia and Amir are with me. We're evaluating runtimes for low-latency generative features and considering on-prem for data residency.
[00:14] Sofia: hi all, sound good.
[00:16] Carlos: quick agenda: kernel selection, tensor cores/FP16 vs INT8 quantization, TensorRT-LLM integration, vLLM path differences, CUDA Graphs for warm paths, and KV cache/batching behavior. We'll show traces and heuristics.
[00:30] Amir: Great — our main constraints: sub-100ms tail P95 for 256-token prompts, but cost matters; want to understand when Dedicated or Private makes sense.
[00:42] Maya: perfect. quick qual: what's your current infra? cloud? on-prem? hybrid?
[00:48] Liam: we're hybrid — sagemaker for most training, but inference will sit in our data center; GPUs are A100 80GB. We also use an internal redis for short-term caching.
[00:58] Carlos: A100 80GB is a good baseline. Are you running FP16 inference today?
[01:03] Sofia: we tried FP16; model had some instability so we rolled back to FP32 in prod. looking at INT8 quant for cost.
[01:12] Carlos: ok noted. We'll talk about per-op kernel choices — e.g., fused attention kernels vs cuBLAS matmuls — and when TensorRT-LLM gives advantage over a vLLM path.

[01:30] Carlos: (shares screen) Here's a trace from a 13B model with 256 context. Left is vLLM-like scheduling: many small kernel launches, dynamic dispatch and per-layer attention kernels. Right is TensorRT-LLM optimized pass with kernel fusion and attention pattern kernels, fewer launches, and more work per kernel.
[01:55] Sofia: I see a lot of small kernels on the left. Does that explain larger tail variance?
[02:02] Carlos: yeah, small kernels and frequent host-device syncs raise variance. vLLM is good for flexible scheduling and memory efficient KV cache handling but at high frequency you can get fragmentation and launcher overhead.
[02:15] Nina: also vLLM's allocator behavior interacts with large KV caches; if you have many concurrent sessions the allocator may cause additional cudaMalloc/cudaFree churn unless you use a pooled allocator.
[02:30] Amir: we do keep persistent streams and a pooled allocator but still hit some spikes at P95. Any quick wins?
[02:37] Carlos: CUDA Graphs for the hot path — capture the forward pass and replay — reduces kernel launch overhead and flattens latency. But it's brittle if your sequence lengths vary a lot or you need dynamic shapes.
[02:49] Liam: our traffic has mostly short prompts (~40 tokens) and occasional long ones (500+). How would you handle mixed shape?
[02:58] Carlos: typical approach: tiered graphs. Precompile graphs for common lengths (16, 32, 64, 128, 256) and fall back to a dynamic path for outliers. Also prefix/KV cache helps — if a long response is generated incrementally you don't re-run the entire context.

[03:20] Sofia: on quantization: when is INT8 safe? we worry about quality regression.
[03:25] Carlos: INT8 can work but you need per-channel calibration and sometimes row-wise quant for attention kernels. TensorRT-LLM has tuned INT8 kernels and calibrators; vLLM path often relies on custom F32/FP16 kernels unless you patch in quant kernels. For strict quality we recommend a per-prompt eval suite.
[03:40] Maya: quick real-world note: our Optimize toolkit will recommend quant profiles per model and run quality regression checks tied to your eval set so you can see delta in hallucination/likelihood metrics.
[03:52] Amir: good to hear. on Dedicated vs Private — if we want on-prem, how does Redwood handle kernel selection? is it automated?
[04:00] Nina: the runtime uses a kernel selection pass at model load time that benchmarks several candidate kernels per operator pattern on your hardware and picks the best. For some ops it records heuristics (sequence length, batch size) and switches at runtime if the distribution changes.
[04:15] Liam: how long does that benchmarking take? we can't have long startup times in production restarts.
[04:20] Carlos: usually a few minutes per model for a thorough pass; there is a fast-path that samples fewer configs and finishes in under 30s. We persist a kernel-profile and ship it to a config store; on autoscale new nodes download the profile.
[04:32] Sofia: what about compatibility with CUDA Graphs? if we pick different kernels at runtime, do graphs need re-capture?
[04:38] Carlos: good question. If you change the kernel mix post-capture you need to re-capture the graph; our workflow is: pick a stable kernel set for hot paths, capture CUDA Graphs for those, and mark variant kernels as non-graph (fallback). The runtime can route outliers to non-graph path.
[04:54] Amir: we care about tail behavior. can you share empirical numbers?
[05:00] Carlos: sure — this is representative: for 13B on A100 80GB with batch=1 and 256 context, vLLM path (no graph, FP16) P50=23ms P95=112ms P99=180ms. With TensorRT-LLM fused kernels + CUDA Graphs + FP16, P50=18ms P95=72ms P99=120ms. With INT8 tuned kernels in TensorRT-LLM, we see P50=14ms P95=55ms but quality delta varies per model. These are representative; will share spreadsheet.
[05:25] Sofia: those are big improvements. how about concurrent throughput?
[05:29] Carlos: with batching and a good KV cache, throughput improves linearly until memory becomes the bottleneck. Also, the runtime can multiplex requests with prefix caching so you don't repeat work for similar prompts.
[05:42] Liam: we use a lot of cached prompts internally; would Redwood integrate with our Redis cache or does it use an in-process KV store?
[05:49] Nina: we support both. For Private deployments we can plug into your Redis or provide a local LRU KV cache. For Dedicated we run an in-process/high-speed KV by default.
[05:59] Amir: on security/compliance: we need KMS integration and audit logs, and possibly air-gapped. Is that covered?
[06:05] Maya: yes — Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations, full audit logs, SSO, and on-prem appliance for air-gapped. We'll attach SOC2 and compliance docs.
[06:15] Liam: thanks.

[06:20] Carlos: ok back to kernel selection heuristics. Two main levers: fused attention (fewer kernels, more memory per op) vs split kernels (memory efficient, more launches). For large sequence lengths fused attention often wins in latency, but memory can blow up. We pick based on available memory headroom.
[06:38] Sofia: memory headroom—how do you estimate with KV cache? we keep long-term histories for some users.
[06:44] Carlos: we simulate worst-case concurrency: (max concurrent sessions) * (per-session KV size) + model weights + workspace. Our planner flags configs likely to cause OOM and will favor split kernels for those nodes. You can tune policies to favor latency vs capacity.
[06:58] Amir: what about multi-GPU sharding? we do model parallel for >70B models but we're testing 13B and 70B variants.
[07:06] Carlos: for multi-GPU the kernel selection includes NCCL-friendly patterns and kernel fusion that's cross-GPU aware where possible. TensorRT-LLM has good NVLink-aware kernels; vLLM can work but may need custom all-reduce tuning. We'll document specifics in the spreadsheet.

[07:30] Nina: now a short demo — here's a nvprof timeline of repeated captures. Notice that after we enable CUDA Graphs the timeline shows fewer host-to-device transitions and more contiguous GPU work. tail latency tightens.
[07:50] Sofia: does graph replay increase determinism at scale?
[07:53] Carlos: yes, capture/replay gives much more deterministic kernel scheduling and reduces syscalls. But you must pick conservative memory footprints for graphs; if a graph needs more temporary memory at runtime it will fail to replay.
[08:07] Liam: talking about variabilities, we saw jitter when many small chat sessions hit the same host. Any guidance on isolation?
[08:14] Nina: run per-tenant pools or cgroup isolation, and prefer Dedicated with pinned capacity for predictable tail SLOs. For Private on-prem, you can set node allocation policies to avoid noisy neighbor effects.

[08:30] Amir: could you run a proof-of-concept on our hardware? we can give you access for a short pilot.
[08:34] Maya: absolutely. typical pilot: you provide a model binary and traces, we run tensor- and kernel-selection pass, then a set of microbenchmarks (CUDA Graphs capture, int8 calibration, KV cache stress) and share results.
[08:47] Sofia: timeline?
[08:49] Maya: if you drop artifacts this week we can run microbenchmarks and get a spreadsheet back within 3 business days.
[08:55] Liam: good. cost question — how much effort and cost for Dedicated vs Private pilot?
[09:00] Maya: pilot compute cost is covered by Redwood for initial PoC if you sign an NDA; Dedicated pricing will be modelled in the spreadsheet and depends on reserved GPU hours. We'll include a TCO comparison and expected per-token cost under the suggested config.
[09:14] Amir: ok good.

[09:20] Carlos: a couple engineering caveats: 1) mixed precision requires per-op lossless checks; 2) INT8 often needs per-layer recalibration and can change attention kernels; 3) quantization + CUDA Graphs is doable but you need careful graph invalidation handling.
[09:36] Sofia: can you explain graph invalidation handling?
[09:39] Carlos: when the runtime detects a kernel switch or a change in workspace size that would violate the captured graph assumptions, it can either invalidate graphs and re-capture (expensive) or route that session to non-graph fallback. We tend to favor marking graphs as static for hot routes and use fallback for the rest.
[09:53] Liam: any real example of when we should prefer vLLM path?
[09:58] Carlos: vLLM is often better when your workload has highly dynamic shapes, lots of on-the-fly token-level ops, or extreme memory constraints. If you need the lowest possible P95 for stable shapes, TensorRT-LLM + graphs typically wins.
[10:12] Maya: quick check — your quality bar for rollout is P95<100ms for typical prompts, and minimal QA delta for LLM outputs?
[10:19] Amir: yes, and we need auditability and KMS.
[10:22] Maya: noted.

[10:25] Carlos: final notes: we'll run three experiments: 1) baseline vLLM FP16 path; 2) TensorRT-LLM fused kernels FP16 + graphs; 3) TensorRT-LLM INT8 calibration. For each we'll provide P50/P95/P99, memory usage, and perf counters. We'll also include kernel-selection logs.
[10:43] Sofia: perfect. one more: can Redwood run inside our VPC with private control plane?
[10:48] Nina: yes — Redwood Private supports VPC peering, private control plane, and an on-prem appliance option. We'll include network diagrams in the follow-up.

[10:58] Amir: last quick question — any known issues on A100 80GB we should watch for?
[11:02] Carlos: on A100 watch workspace fragmentation with fused attention; we recommend at least one big pooled workspace allocator and tuning max_batch + max_seq to avoid fragmentation. Also keep driver/runtime versions in alignment with TensorRT versions.
[11:14] Liam: great. thanks team.

[11:18] Maya: recap of next steps: Maya will share the benchmark spreadsheet and perf traces; Carlos will run the CUDA Graphs microbenchmark on Aegis sample; Liam will provide model and traces; schedule follow-up. We'll draft a short pilot plan.
[11:33] Amir: thanks everyone.

[11:36] (meeting ends)
